items.body:
Sunn O))) guest players and Ideologic Organ mainstays Jessika Kenney and Eyvind Kang return with six new pieces for voice, viola, setar and electronics.

Recorded in Istanbul, Seattle and Bologna, The Face Of The Earth is more obviously Eastern in tone to the duo's last IO offering, Aestuarium. Taking its cue from classical Persian and Javanese traditions, and themed around the idea of "drawing the binary from the unary, like reflections from a mirror, and its inverse, the concealed identity", it's a collection of sonic riddles whose meaning can be unlocked, at least to some extent, by the "reading cards" provided in the insert. Despite the arcane mysticism at work, it's music of self-evident and ravishing beauty: from the medievalist balladry of 'Tavaf', to the pensive but restlessly percussive 'Kidung', Kenney's vocal performances are show-stopping throughout, and Kang's strings resonate powerfully around them. Over its short duration, the sparse voice and viola interplay of 'Ordered Pairs II' take on the character of spiritual jazz, while the looping and phasing techniques applied on 'Mirror Stage' come over like a courtly response to Steve Reich's 'It's Gonna Rain', and 'The Face Of The Earth' feels like the logical extension of the more avant-garde moments on Julia Holter's Ekstasis. Tremendous stuff.

items.body:
Psych duo Bear Bones, Lay Low naturally adapt to soundtrack dimensions with a richly atmospheric, electroacoustic accompaniment to Léonard Pongo’s titular film, benefitting from Laszlo Umbreit’s experience in this arena.

“Discrepant presents the LP edition of Tales from the Source, the original film soundtrack by Bear Bones, Lay Low and Laszlo Umbreit. Originally composed for Belgian-Congolese artist Léonard Pongo’s 2024 film of the same name, this release reworks the film's audio into a continuous, fluid listening experience.

The album is built on a direct contrast between heavy electronic manipulation and raw environmental audio. Laszlo Umbreit captured the foundation of the record through field recordings and additional electronics, focusing on the quiet, tactile sounds of water, riverbeds, and natural spaces. These recordings were then processed and expanded by Bear Bones, Lay Low, who layered the tracks using synthesizers, samplers and various effects processors.

Rather than acting as a standard background score, the music functions as a detailed piece of environmental sound art. The tracks are edited to blend into one another without distinct gaps, mirroring the slow pace and visual flow of the film. Through the use of tape loops, filtering, and electronic processing, the natural landscapes are systematically distorted and rearranged. The result is a dark, slow-moving suite of electroacoustic music that strips away traditional melody to focus entirely on texture, resonance, and the changing dynamics of the recorded environments.”

items.body:
2nd wave dub techno staple Stephen Hitchell meets new wave producer Federson in a back ’n forth of timeless originals and versions.

San Francisco’s Chris Kelly, aka Federsen’s Alt Dub label hosts this passing of the baton/torch with CV313 and Echospace figure Hitchell a sits 2nd release after the ‘Positive Charge’ EP  christened the vessel in earlier ’24. Federsen fronts the session with a smoky, night-driving dub of CV313’s ‘Skycrossing’ in properly classic Maurizio style, especially that scooping bassline, whilst shutting it down with the more air-stepping levity of his dusted congas and distant dub chords to ‘Skyway’.

CV313’s original ‘Skycrossing’ places his mastery of constantly shifting, ever the same, dynamic within its unfurling envelopes, alongside a remix of ‘Skyway’ that plunges upward, outward into billowing electro-acoustic dub techno dimensions.

items.body:
Tobias Freund’s roots in ‘80s & ‘90s pop engineering - for Milli Vanilli, Meat Loaf, Scatman John! - are touched-up in a 2nd parade of cover versions, of The Human League, This Heat, Japan, Suicide, Heaven 17, and Harold Budd & Brian Eno

Perhaps best known to many for his run of classic ’00s minimal techno as Tobias., the German producer’s binds run much deeper than that sound, with engineering credits on the likes of Lassigue Bendthaus’ pivotal EBM album ‘Matter’, as well as those that paid the bills (Milli Vanilli, Meat Loaf). ‘Plenty Of Time With Nothing To Do’ now catches him returning to formative passions with ample technical knowledge earned over the decades, generating a mix of faithful and daring takes on evergreens and personal faves augmented with inventive, playful nuance.

Tobias.’ freunds are vocal foils, with Barbie Williams perfectly emulating Andrea Conway’s dreamy delivery of Dome’s ‘Cruel When Complete’, subtly reset in dusty triplets, while Romina Schopf drily glazes the tribal groove of their take on This Heat’s ‘Twilight Furniture’, and Argenis Brito channels David Sylvian with a Latin accent in the re-do of Japan’s ‘My New Career’. The ‘floor is also attended on Gudrun Gut’s standout, breathy revision of Suicide’s ‘Girl’, and Tobias. himself even makes an appearance, pitched alien-like on a puckered revision of The Human League’s ‘Morale’, another highpoint along with Uwe Schmidt aka Atom™ reprising his LB ‘Pop Artificielle’ steez on a remake of Heaven 17’s ‘The Best Kept Secret’.

items.body:
Skewed dub specialist label Blundar host a mutant cumbia dub haunting by Bogotá’s ezmeralda, a leading figure of wayward ambient shook up from the Latin American bush of ghosts...

Preceded by an LP for Tra Tra Trax’s Ambie-Tón divison, and an EP with Éter Editions, ezmeralda continues to stake out a unique sort of tresillo metaphysics perhaps familiar to fans of Debit’s Modern Love albums or Elijah Minnelli fancies, or even The Caretaker’s slant on dusty ballroom standards, but applied to traditional cumbia. Everything inside is slowed and diffused to a vaporous crawl; bone-rubbed rhythms and basslines smudged into oblivion, and air hashed with spectral traces of flutes and accordions; ancient cries heard thru a modern lens.

For 16 minutes ezmeralda suspends perceptions of time and space with a sublime, deferred gratification, never quite fully revealing the forms, operating by suggestion in finely extracted and layered arrangements. The A-side feels as though we’re shored-up on some Mangrove-covered Caribbean coastline of Colombia at night, threats lurking below the briny surface and thick in the air, before the B-side brings the phantoms forward in what feels like Pole processing Elijah Minnelli’s anachronistic cumbia blooz...

items.body:
DJ Sprinkles' classic Midtown 120 Blues, self-released by Terre Thaemlitz through their Comatonse imprint and finally available again.

Bringing deep house back into contact with its club culture roots, Terre Thaemlitz created one of the most essential house albums of the last two decades with 'Midtown 120 Blues'. Terre was originally working as a DJ under her Sprinkles alias in the gay clubs of midtown Manhattan and New Jersey in the late 80's when deep house began to blossom. It's this early period of House history which Terre has beautifully recreated over 10 tracks, making a pointed comment with the intro track taking shots at Strictly Rhythm for becoming 'Strictly Vocal' and pulling no punches towards "Most Europeans who think deep house means shitty hi-NRG vocal house".

With the intentions made clear, Terre develops a masterpiece of serene melancholy and sublime deep house crafted with the skill and dedication of someone who you know lived this music through every fibre of their being. From the rich subbass driven tones of 'Midtown 120 Blues' with plaintive pianos slowly encircling one another, to drag queen monologues over the deepest ambient brushed rhythms on 'Ball'r (Madonna-Free Zone)' or head-meltingly warm chords and caressed percussion of 'Brenda's $20 dilemna' - this will suck in and swallow you whole -  transporting you to another place, another time.

A total pleasure.

items.body:
Remastered reissue of This Heat’s hugely innovative and pioneering anti-rock classic, 1979,  this time on their own, eponymous label. A true milestone in the mutation of pop, rock, avant-garde and electronic music, and arguably post-punk's ground-zero, This Heat consolidated a wealth of music before its arrival whilst casting irrevocable influence over a generation of musicians, producers and engineers in its wake.

Formed in mid ‘70s Brixton, South London, around the trio of Charles Hayward, Charles Bullen and Gareth Williams (later of Flaming Tunes fame), the group drew on and experimented within a flux of sonic disciplines - concrète, pop, dub, and krautrock - to align their mutual ligaments and oppositional structures in a complex, dissonant mass of finely edited improvisations.

Spooling tape noise Testcards jar abruptly with bursts of taut, buzzing drums and metallic guitar squall in Horizontal Hold, before Williams appears as a lamenting ghost, wallowing in the funereal folk drone of Not Waving, and like Damo Suzuki’s shy opposite against the motorik flight of Twilight Furniture.

The album’s definitive moment is still to come, however, with the 2-bar lick of Hayward’s propulsive drums spun thru devilish reverbs and delays in the legendary 24 Track Loop marking a pivotal moment in flux between dub, punk and electro-acoustic music, before the record closes out with Fall of Saigon’s melancholy dirge pop, which clearly set a template for everyone from Hot Chip to Animal Collective or Micachu and the Shapes.

Perhaps understandably, This Heat were never intended as a commercial proposition but, thru the support of John Peel they were able to reach and beguile a national radio audience who probably weren’t ready for them. Thus, their boundary-oblivious virus was planted in the fertile minds of ’79, when punk had already eaten itself and new ideas were definitely required.

By using a minimalist, rhythmically-focussed palette, rent by great minds using the studio-as-instrument, This Heat represents a crucial transition or phase-shift in music from stratified styles toward a union of what might have been formerly perceived as mutually exclusive sounds or styles; boldly following a path out of genre restriction and dilating the dimensions of sonic possibility in the process.

A stone cold classic.

items.body:
Following 2024's avant-prog-Americana song cycle 'Viewfinder', guitar deity Wendy Eisenberg goes chamber pop on their self-titled latest, tipping their hat to Judee Sill, Gillian Welch, Van Dyke Parks and Joanna Newsom.

When they relocated from rural Western Mass to Brooklyn in 2020, Eisenberg was hit with a wave of longing for the open landscape they'd left behind. They were drawn to classic country and folk records, perfectly poised offerings from Willie Nelson and John Hartford and lavish pop-folk records from Jimmy Webb and Van Dyke Parks as well as the weirdo fare of Richard Dawson et al. So when 'Viewfinder', a way of deconstructing the experience following eye surgery in 2011, was finished, Eisenberg started writing "genuinely folk songs" and swapping out their usually showy, complex performance for a form of relative simplicity that they explain is inherently strange all the same. Prog becomes folk, basically. And they're not on their own; more eaze handles the lush string arrangements, playing pedal steel and synthesizer, and a loose band forms around that axis, with drummer Ryan Sawyer and bassist Trevor Dunn.

But despite the personnel, it's resolutely Eisenberg's album. Their voice sounds unrestrained, capturing the era they're referencing and their own emotional (and physical upheaval). It's fragile but strangely warm on the country-tinged Jim O'Rourke-like 'Will You Dare' and hypnotic on the baroque 'Meaning Business', a track they wrote in the wake of David Lynch's death as the antithesis of the "Lynchian" aesthetic. And they should really get their flowers for this one; Americana, especially now, is teetering on a precipice, almost knocked off the edge by half-assed, churned attempts and underwritten pastiches. Eisenberg's an attentive listener and someone who's surrounded themself with similarly sensitive ears, people who are able to fill their heart and their sound so what we hear is as byzantine as a Gastr del Sol record but sounds as effortless as John Prine's 'Angel From Montgomery'. If you loved Joanna Newsom's 'Ys' and have never found anything quite as satisfying, this is the one.

The unstoppable LIV.e finds her groove alongside Stones Throw mainstay Karriem Riggins on 'The Pleasure is Yours', breathing life into a set of big hearted contemporary avant-soul/hip-hop experiments that'll hit anyone into Erykah Badu's 'New Amerykah' tomes.

Riggins is an old hand at this stage. The bandleader for Common's old band, he's produced alongside Dilla, worked with The Roots and Ye, collaborated with Madlib and kept it fresh by breaking bread with Kaytranada, Denzel Curry and Earl Sweatshirt. And if you're used to poring through the liners, you'll realize it was his mind behind Badu's 'Soldier', one of the highlights from her second-wind classic 'New Amerykah Part One'. It's this hiccuping sound - a rougher, more defiantly hip-hop inspired take on what became sold as "neo soul" - that roots 'The Pleasure is Yours', the first record from Riggins' self-styled supergroup alongside young prodigy Hailee Olivia Williams, aka LIV.e. 

Working with his trusty LinnDrum and playing bass and piano, Riggins orchestrates a backdrop that's knowing (he was there, after all) but oddly relevant - and twice as wonked as anything from his younger rivals. For her part, LIV.e adds the charm and the warmth. We already know she's good - it's not just hype - and her songs crackle, purr and flicker alongside Riggins' skittering beats. On one level, it's pure psych - tune into the rattly, swirling 'TGD' and tell us it ain't - but what makes this one stand out is that it never takes itself too seriously. So we're treated to brash Prince-style belters like 'This is so Crazy', the waved Motown-like 'DoobieDooWew' and the levitational 'You've Outdone Yourself Today, Huh?' all on one record.

Their third album, ‘Treasure’ also debuts Simon Raymonde on bass and finds the band scaling new heights in the most emotionally raw way imaginable. Impossible to overstate just how influential and well loved this album is - from the quietly anthemic Pandora (For Cindy) - probably played in every bedroom by every teenager in 1984, to the sublime 'Beatrix' and 'Otterley' - tracks that were played on Autechre’s Disengage Kiss FM show in the early 90’s and which gave us our first introduction to one of the most magical and timeless albums ever made.

"The band returned to being a trio in 1984 with guitarist Simon Raymonde joining their ranks in time for third album, Treasure. Produced by Robin Guthrie and featuring tracks ‘Lorelei’, ‘Ivo’ and ‘Persephone’, Treasure is often celebrated as one of the band’s finest works. As Pitchfork put it when including the album in their Top 100 Albums of the 1980s, “Treasure was titled simply enough. An adjective for the endlessly inventive melodic lines you'd find buried in these songs, and a verb for what you'd do with them for years to come.”

items.body:
The most perfectly formed Cocteau Twins album, perhaps one of the most perfectly formed albums of all time - soaked in bittersweet sorrow and nostalgia, it’s almost painful listening to it 30 years later.

Numerous publications have declared it one of the best albums of the 90s, with Pitchfork calling it “a core of ungodly gorgeous songs that is every bit as moving and relevant today as it ever was.”. Famously - 4AD founder Ivo Watts-Russell has called it his favourite all-time 4AD album, “by a long shot”. 

Recorded in the midst of much upheaval - the birth of Fraser and Guthrie's daughter, the death of Simon Raymonde’s father Ivor Raymonde, the disintegration of the band’s relationship with 4AD (this was to be their last album for the label) - the result is lucid and enveloping, you can even decipher some of Fraser’s lyrics on this one.

Anyway, Heaven or Las Vegas is really one of life’s great pleasures for anyone acquainted with it. And if you aren’t - get to it.

Sferic/Faitiche emissary Roméo Poirier pairs up with stylistic mentor Jan Jelinek on a sampler's delight, answering Jelinek's romantic 2005 gem 'Collage of Digital Passion' with a montaged mirror image that fizzes with plunderphonic warmth.

Jelinek has been using The Exposures pseudonym since 2003, most notably pillaging micro-samples from numerous R&B records on "Collage Of Digital Passion” issued by Prefuse 73’s Eastern Developments label back in 2005. In his by-now inimitable loop-finding style, that track has become a bit of a low-slung classic, reminding us not only of his iconic productions of the early 2000’s, but also of Anthony Shakir’s iconic ‘Mr. Shakir's Beat Store’ from just a couple of years earlier.

For his “version”, Poirier flips “I hate you!" samples with fanciful, theatrical soundscapes that ooze warmth, capturing the essence of Jelinek's original perfectly.

items.body:
Remastered from the original tapes by Robin Guthrie and reissued on vinyl for the first time, 'The Moon and the Melodies' is one of the Cocteau Twins' most sublime sets, a blissful marriage of horizontal piano-laced ambience and glistening dream pop.

"It's not Cocteau Twins, and it's not me," Budd said in a 1986 interview, "it's an odd combination peculiar to the mixture." He'd never heard the band until bassist Simon Raymonde reached out to cover 'Not Yet Remembered' from his 'Ambient 2: Plateaux of Mirror' collaboration with Brian Eno. Although the cover never materialised, Budd was struck by the trio's music and after a meeting in Los Angeles, they began to consider a full collaboration. 'The Moon and the Melodies' appeared at a good time, Budd had recently released his syrupy masterpiece 'The Pearl', and Cocteau Twins had sailed further into abstraction with their beatless oddity 'Victorialand'. The album also marked the end of an era for Guthrie, Raymonde and Liz Fraser, catching them on the cusp of their later shift towards more identifiable pop, and integrating Budd's signature languid piano worked seamlessly. Just check 'Memory Gongs', still one of the most pristine entries in either act's repertoire - seven and a half minutes of rubbery, tremolo piano reverberations and muggy, billowing soundscapes. 

But the big draw will no doubt be opener 'Sea, Swallow Me', a more recognisable Cocteaus cut that's had a new lease of life since it became a viral hit on TikTok, of all places. It's now one of the band's most recognisable (and most streamed) songs, and Budd's serene arpeggios take on a slightly different form when they're balanced with Guthrie's shimmering riffs, Raymonde's driving basslines and Fraser's soaring voice. The four alternate between proper songs and ambient reflections, as if they're each paying attention to each other's strengths while attempting to experiment. "It turned out like four songs that sounded like us and four songs that sounded like him, which wasn't really the plan," remembers Guthrie. And it's interesting that when it was originally released, the album was credited to each musician, rather than being listed as a Cocteau Twins album; indeed, Raymonde recalls that the sessions were enjoyably un-premeditated. "It captured a moment in time between friends that are enjoying making music together," he explains. "Really, that's the essence of it."

Elsewhere, Dif Juz's Richard Thomas plays sax on two of the album's most crushing tracks: the jangly, anthemic 'She Will Destroy You' and the cloudy 'The Ghost Has No Home'. The latter is one of the Budd-forward tracks, and stretches into the abyss with his piano fainting into Thomas's echoing horns and Guthrie's tempered, chiming guitar phrases. It's hardly surprising that the album marked the beginning of a collaboration between Guthrie and Budd that would eventually give us the iconic 'Mysterious Skin' soundtrack in 2005.

'The Moon and the Melodies' has never sounded better; it's aged well, pulling away from the expectations that caused some critics to misunderstand it when it emerged almost four decades ago, gradually establishing itself as a stylistic milestone in the years since.

items.body:
Returning after a decade-long break with none other than Isis/Sumac frontman Aaron Turner at the helm, Neurosis move into a new era with their sickest album since the iconic 'Through Silver in Blood'. Tipped!

It would have been easy to assume that Neurosis would have folded after guitarist and vocalist Scott Kelly, one of the band's founder members, was dismissed following domestic abuse allegations. Indeed, as late as in January last year, it looked like things were fizzling out when drummer Jason Roeder claimed he was ready to sell his music equipment and retire from touring. And it would have made sense, too; Neurosis have been active since the mid-1980s and defined a sound that would evolve into "post-metal", pulling influence from hardcore, prog, industrial music, ambient and sludge and inspiring a legion of followers. They never really lost their mojo, either - even their last album, 2016's Steve Albini-recorded 'Fires Within Fires' was pretty universally regarded as one of that year's best metal releases. But truth be told, they'd started to repeat themselves; locked into Kelly's grim, agonized lyrics, they were starting to sound like their own gloomy tribute act. If it was the end, they'd had a good run.

So 'An Undying Love...' is in many senses a total surprise Not only is the band back, re-energised, but they have a new vocalist and guitarist in tow: Turner, whose old band Isis were arguably the most important members of post-metal's second wave. You might consider the new Neurosis lineup as the ultimate post-metal supergroup, then, and 'An Undying Love...' is the record that proves the credentials of everyone involved. Unlike its tight, almost too brief predecessor, this album is a return to the epic, sprawling songwriting that both Neurosis and Isis perfected at their respective peaks. And it's incredibly expansive, too; anyone who's been following Turner in recent years will already know how open-minded he is, whether it's with his work with Moor Mother and Keiji Haino as Sumac or his various genre-bending collaborations. Here, there's an extra layer to the Neurosis sound that fills out their sludgy, lurching epics with the meticulously engineered haze of Isis's milestone 'Oceanic'.

Where Neurosis's last few albums had been shaped by their long-time collaboration with Albini, this one sounds like a clean break, mixed and recorded by Oakland's Scott Evans, who worked on Turner's Sumac records. It's still Neurosis, with those slow, almost symphonic atmospheres and the unmistakably tight rhythm section, but there's even more going on here, whether it's the unsettlingly effective breakdowns that often replace the band's usual instruments with synths and pounding drum machines, or the stacked feedback loops and scratches that fill their riffs with even more tension. Turner's lyrics, too, offer the band a new dimension to explore. "The separation that burns our hearts / is the root of all our disease," he bellows on the opener 'We Are Torn Wide Open' over radio interference. "We've forgotten how to live so we suffer." Self-referential in their own way at first, they move on as the band does, rolling through themes of environmental collapse, division and redemption. 

It's worth it just for the payoff delivered by the album's side-long finale 'Last Light', shifting from hi-BPM dark gabber into pure symphonic sludge, using its hefty runtime to properly display what this nu-Neurosis (NeurIsis?) is capable of. Really, it's not just the band's most vital record in years, it's one of the best metal albums we've heard in way, way too long.

Will Long dons his dancing slippers for another deep house sojourn on his Long Trax Productions, blowing kisses in the direction of Larry Heard, Ron Trent, DJ Sprinkles.

One decade since minting the ‘Long Trax’ series on Terre Thaemlitz’s label, Comatonse, Will Long slow cooks six new additions on his personal folio, taking all the time needed to get right into the groove. Trust there’s no fireworks or over-produced trickery, just hypnotic deep house that unfurls with a real sense of space, patience and deferred gratification.

Long in his element, following his nose to pair the barest ingredients in classic style and pattern, as with with the likes of ‘About Where It's At (Now You Went N' Did It mix)’, which takes over 4 mins happily swinging away before introducing its lonesome flute motif, or a standout ‘Have to Have Something’ lost in the flow, where the bassline only thickens as it goes along. 

We’re also partial to the square bass budge of ‘Have To Have Something (S' a Lotta Shade mix)’, and the mesmerising meld of creamy bass and piquant cowbell pinging on ‘The Problems’, also found warped with trippier effect on its Metallic Dub reshape.

Autechre's reissue engine reaches their outstanding 2008 album, featuring definitive moments of their near 40 year (and ongoing) run.

‘Quaristice’ is Rob Brown and Sean Booth’s 9th studio album as Autechre, conceived some 20 years up-to-the-hilt in their thing, and depicting the duo emerging into a sort of hybrid live x studio jam style that’s distinguished much of their work thus far. However archänlèy, it’s still not even the best version - that honour is reserved to the 2.5hr digital-only ‘Quaristice.Quadrange.ep.ae’ brimming with extended versions, including an hour long mix of ‘Perlance subrange 6-36’ and deadly 10’ mix of ‘Tkakanren’ - but suffice it to say we’re made up to see this one in the wild on vinyl, at least.

The follow-up to a pivotal standout, 2004’s ‘Untilted’ (also reissued this year), ‘Quaristice’ really felt like a future upgrade to the system on its release in 2008. Completely unconcerned with prevailing or emerging trends of dubstep or UKF at the time, it sees the duo follow their noses for hardware/ software jams into the proper mutant body music, milling limbs to the meanest 112BPM electro swag in the twin-rotor electro hip hop gnash of ‘Tankakern’, and utterly wrecking the senses in the blizzard dynamic of ‘Fol3’, or manipulating sinew with deviant liquid B-Boy tekkerz on ’90101-5l-l’ - each of which feature in even better versions on the 2nd disc (and frankly better yet in their alternative extensions of the digi-only version). 

There are flashes of the melodic and harmonically curious Autechre we all know and love in opener ‘Altibzz’ (their love note to the magic of Altrincham), the aerated strings of ‘Theswere’, and almost Lynchian noir of ‘Notwo’, yet the whole thing feels to trigger muscle memories and flashbacks to club physicality, as felt in the corresponding live show at Pure in Manchester at the time. The mad thing is, as judged from recent live show, they still sound as rudely uncompromising and propulsive now, 17 years later, perhaps more than ever

Jan Jelinek and Alan Abrahams of Portable/Bodycode fame come together on perhaps the most substantial new Jelinek project in years - recalling his own classic Gramm and Farben projects with this low-lit set of simmering, frayed House burners. Really stong!

The two were on each other's radars for years, but didn't come in contact properly until Abrahams brought Jelinek to play at one of his Süd Electronic parties, where they began to mull over the idea of a collaboration. Over the years, they built up a rapport; Abrahams would fire over material that Jelinek would work into the stems, slowly building up the confidence to take more and more risks. He began to fixate on Abrahams voice, ignoring the rest of the instrumentation and threaded it through his usual lattice of concrète sounds in a sort of classic Farben mode.

Farben's a good reference point, particularly for 'Forever', the set's housey-est cut. Jelinek explains in the accompanying press release that the raw vocal had reminded him of "classic house" and that's where we start, with jazzy keys gassing up Abrahams' soulful vox. By the time we hit the halfway point, Jelinek's processes have taken over, with buzzing synths and snowballing percussion that create a dense wall of insectoid noise and interference before the track fades dramatically to silence. It's the most propulsive material Jelinek's been involved with for ages; on '87BPM', he sways Abrahams' wordless groans into a trotting, ping pong shuffle and 'All One' does a thing with tape stop melodies and drunken vocals that sound like an offcut from the CMYK series of EPs.

Breezy new age house by an Antipodean artist with illustrious credits beside Michal Hutchence, Bono, Jamiroquai since the ‘80s, evened out with Kuniyuki and 451 remixes...

"Originally emerging from Melbourne’s post-punk and new wave underground in the late 1970s and early 1980s, Gus Till has spent more than four decades navigating a remarkably diverse musical path. From early electronic experimentation with Third Eye alongside Ollie Olsen, through a pivotal role in the formative years of the global psy-trance movement and collaborations with artists including Michael Hutchence, System 7, Manu Dibango, Todd Terry and Bim Sherman, Till’s work has consistently resisted easy categorisation, moving fluidly between ambient music, downtempo, house, trance and psychedelic electronica.

First released on Japan’s Dakini Records in 2006, ‘Rainsong’ captures many of these threads in a single expansive composition. Built around a pulsating bassline, layered live percussion and soaring vocal elements, the track sits comfortably between the dancefloor and more immersive listening environments. Unfolding patiently across nearly thirteen minutes, it combines hypnotic rhythmic momentum with a rich sense of atmosphere and musicality.

For the B-side, Kuniyuki Takahashi offers a distinct reinterpretation of the original. His remix gradually unfolds from a patient introduction into a deep and richly textured exploration of the track’s core themes. Subtle spatial processing, nuanced arrangement shifts and his unmistakable sense of atmosphere transform the source material while preserving its emotional core."

As O.G. Jigg, Will “Memotone” Yates adapts his broad palette to the 16mm documentary and folk horror short imagery of Graham Vasey’s film project, The Black Tor, with an unmistakably vintage tone FFO Oskar Sala, Delia Derbyshire, Gruppo.

Named for the granite outcrop of Dartmoor, not too far from the musician’s native Bristol, ‘Black Tor Tracks’ depicts Yates in actual soundtrack mode, as opposed to imaginary. It gathers six instrumental accompaniments written between 2022-2026 that match the oneiric anachronisms of County Durham based Graham Vasey’s films with masterful blends of analog electronics and acoustic kit rendered in widescreen and dusted with a tone that reflects the filmmaker’s use of a 1950s Bolex and a 1930s Ensign Auto-Kinecam. 

If we weren’t informed otherwise, the music could easily pass for ‘50s or ’60 orchestral scores in a classic vein of British folk horror, or even Bernard Herrmann’s work for Hitchcock psychological thrillers - and by extension, even Oskar Sala in its electronic nuance - such is the timeless quality of Yates’ touch as O.G. Jigg. Severed from intended imagery the music remains potently synaesthetic, from the gloomy brood of ‘The Black Tor’, thru the celluloid dream sequence evocation of ‘The Sunken Kirk’, fine-wrought early electronic timbres of ‘Woodwose’ and ‘The Stones of Obb’, and hallucinatory tension of ‘Plough Stots’.

Good stuff.

Dutch A/V duo Wanderwelle plunge Davey Jones’ locker in a richly metaphoric expression of worries about climate change and marine devastation, blending hydrophonic acoustic and electronic sources to spell out a sonorous, subaquatic narrative FFO Mark Jenkin film scores, Thomas Köner, AFX’s SAW II...

“After All Hands Bury The Cliffs At Sea (2023) and Black Clouds Above The Bows (2022), Amsterdam-based collective Wanderwelle presents the final entry of their album trilogy for Important Records (IMPREC). Conceived as a sonic reflection on the climate crisis and its devastating impact on coastal ecosystems, Ghosts Beneath The Brine (2026) addresses the mass deaths of fish, seabirds, crustaceans and countless other creatures that call these seas home, now rapidly being overfished, warming and acidifying.

Where antique cavalry trumpets played a central role on Black Clouds Above The Bows and a dying church organ shaped All Hands Bury The Cliffs At Sea, cymbals form the core of Ghosts Beneath The Brine. The instruments were submerged in seawater for extended periods of time and played with a bow at various stages of corrosion. As the bronze alloy gradually reacted with the saltwater, their sound transformed, becoming darker, more fragile and unstable. Over time, the metal began to sing in ghostly overtones, as if haunted by the waters that shaped it. Much like large groups of fish shimmering beneath the surface, the cymbals slowly lost their shine, both sonically and physically, as salt and time took hold.

Alongside its environmental narrative, the album draws from maritime mythology. Echoes of the sea bishop, the kraken, devil whales and sea serpents emerge throughout its soundscape. Once feared and revered, these creatures now exist only in the liminal space between folklore and memory, haunting the collective imagination like omens from a forgotten age. Through immersive textures and submerged harmonies, Wanderwelle intertwines myth and mourning, inviting listeners to drift between the real and the spectral. If humanity continues on its current course, familiar species such as sharks, oysters and even gulls may soon share the same fate as their legendary predecessors, becoming ghosts beneath the brine.”
